bib.title: Chapter 7: n-step Bootstrapping (Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.)

question: How can Monte Carlo and one-step TD methods be unified into a spectrum of n-step methods for prediction, on-policy control and off-policy control?
hypothesis: Intermediate amounts of bootstrapping typically perform better than either extreme (MC or one-step TD).
contributions: n-step Sarsa and n-step Expected Sarsa
off-policy n-step learning with importance sampling
per-decision off-policy returns with control variates
n-step Q(sigma) unifying Sarsa, Expected Sarsa and tree backup

results.claim: The expected n-step return has worst-state error at most gamma^n times that of the current value estimate (error reduction property), so n-step TD converges.
results.setup: Eq 7.3, any n >= 1, fixed policy pi, prediction of v_pi
results.quote: the worst error of the expected n-step return is guaranteed to be less than or equal to γn times the worst error under Vt+n−1

results.claim: On the 19-state random walk, intermediate n works best for n-step TD, better than either one-step TD or Monte Carlo (numeric RMS values only appear in Fig 7.2, not in the text).
results.metric: RMS error over 19 states, first 10 episodes
results.setup: 19-state random walk, -1 outcome on left, +1 right, values initialised to 0; n in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512} swept against alpha; error averaged over first 10 episodes and 100 repetitions (same walks for all settings)
results.quote: Note that methods with an intermediate value of n worked best.
results.note: Figure axis labels in the text dump list n=1,2,4,8,16,32,64 and 128,256,512; the legend is garbled so the exact n set is read from Fig 7.2, not stated in prose

results.claim: The 19-state random-walk protocol: 10 episodes, 100 repetitions, 19 states.
results.setup: 19-state random walk, error measured at end of each episode against true values
results.quote: averaged over the ﬁrst 10 episodes and 100 repetitions of the whole experiment

results.claim: In a gridworld, 10-step Sarsa strengthens the last 10 actions on a path to the goal after one episode while one-step Sarsa strengthens only the last action.
results.setup: Fig 7.4: all values initially 0, zero reward except positive reward at G, single episode
results.quote: The one-step method strengthens only the last action of the sequence of actions that led to the high reward, whereas the n-step method strengthens the last n actions of the sequence

results.claim: Importance sampling gives sound off-policy learning but high-variance updates, forcing small step sizes and slow learning; control variates reduce variance.
results.quote: also results in high variance updates, forcing the use of a small step-size parameter and thereby causing learning to be slow

results.claim: With importance sampling if pi never takes an action in the n steps, the whole n-step return gets zero weight; with the control-variate return the target then equals the current estimate (no change).
results.quote: if ⇢t is zero, then instead of the target being zero and causing the estimate to shrink, the target is the same as the estimate and causes no change

results.claim: Tree-backup is the multi-step extension of Q-learning with stochastic target policies and uses no importance sampling, but bootstrapping may span only a few steps if target and behaviour policies differ a lot.
results.quote: the bootstrapping may span only a few steps even if n is large

results.claim: n-step methods delay updates by n steps and need more computation and memory per step than one-step methods.
results.quote: All n-step methods involve a delay of n time steps before updating

limits: No numeric results in the text: the n versus alpha curves exist only in Fig 7.2, whose values are not in the extracted text.
Only the 19-state random walk is run; no experiments for Sarsa, importance sampling, tree backup or Q(sigma) (Q(sigma) described as new to this text).
Authors concede importance-sampling methods are high variance and probably not the most efficient; Q(sigma) not empirically evaluated here.
Tabular setting only; function approximation and eligibility traces deferred to Chapter 12.
practices: Pick an intermediate n rather than one-step TD or Monte Carlo; best results on the random walk were at intermediate n (Ex 7.1, p.145).
For off-policy n-step state values, use the control-variate return (7.13) rather than weighting the whole return by rho (Sec 7.4).
For action values, importance-sample only actions after the first, since the first is already taken (Eq 7.11, p.149).
Use tree backup when off-policy learning without importance sampling is wanted and policies are not very different (Sec 7.5, 7.7).
Use Q(sigma) to interpolate per step between sampling and expectation (Sec 7.6).

terms.definition: Gt:t+n = Rt+1 + γRt+2 + ... + γ^(n-1)Rt+n + γ^n V_{t+n-1}(St+n); equals Gt if t+n >= T
the term (1-ρt)V_{h-1}(St) in the off-policy return; does not change expected update
update from the estimated action values of leaf nodes of the tree, each weighted by its probability under the target policy
per-step degree of sampling σt in [0,1]; σ=1 full sampling (Sarsa), σ=0 pure expectation (tree backup)

code.snippet: Gt:t+n = Rt+1 + γRt+2 + ... + γ^(n-1) Rt+n + γ^n V_{t+n-1}(St+n)
Gt:h = ρt (Rt+1 + γ Gt+1:h) + (1 - ρt) V_{h-1}(St)
τ <- t - n + 1; if τ>=0: G <- sum_{i=τ+1}^{min(τ+n,T)} γ^(i-τ-1) R_i; if τ+n<T: G <- G + γ^n V(S_{τ+n}); V(S_τ) <- V(S_τ)+α[G-V(S_τ)]
